Surah At-Taghabun (The Mutual Loss and Gain)

Medinan according to most scholars, though Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAta' ibn Yasar said it is Meccan except for some of its final verses, from His words ﴿O you who believe, indeed among your spouses﴾ [At-Taghabun: 14] and so on. Its number of verses is nineteen, without disagreement. Its connection to what precedes it is that He, glory be to Him, there mentioned the state of the hypocrites and then addressed the believers. Here He, exalted is He, mentions the division of people into believer and disbeliever. Also, at the end of that surah is ﴿Let neither your wealth nor your children distract you﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 9], and in this surah is ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [At-Taghabun: 15]; this sentence, as has been said, serves as a reason (ta'lil) for that one. Also, in the mention of at-taghabun (mutual loss and gain) there is a kind of urging to spend before death, which was commanded earlier. Some scholars have derived that the age of the Prophet (ﷺ) was sixty-three from His words, exalted is He, in that surah: ﴿And Allah will not delay a soul when its term has come﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 11]; for it is the beginning of the sixty-third surah. He, glory be to Him, followed it with At-Taghabun so that the loss would become evident in his absence, upon him be blessings and peace.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾: that is, all created beings declare Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He, free of whatever is unfitting for the sublimity of His majesty, with continuous glorification. This is by their indicating His perfection, mighty and majestic is He, and His self-sufficiency, exalted is He. The renewal (of this glorification) is by way of the renewed consideration of the aspects of the indication of that.

﴿To Him belongs dominion, and to Him belongs praise﴾: not to anyone else, exalted is He, since He, majestic is His state, is the originator of everything, the one who sustains it and watches over it. He, mighty and majestic, is the master of the roots and branches of blessings. As for the dominion of anyone other than Him, glory be to Him, it is a trust (istirea') and empowerment from Him, exalted is He. As for the praise of anyone other than Him, blessed and exalted is He, it is because His favor flows through his hand. So both matters belong to Him, exalted is He, in reality, and to others according to outward appearance. The mention of ﴿To Him belongs dominion﴾ first is because it serves as evidence for what follows.

﴿And He is over all things Competent﴾: because the relation of His essence, majestic is His state, which entails power, to all things is equal, so it is not conceivable that some things are capable of being done while others are not.

[p. 120]

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿He it is who created you﴾ and so on, are an explanation of part of His general power, Exalted is He. The meaning is: He it is who brought you into existence as He willed. His words, ﴿so among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾, mean: some of you disbelieve in Him, Exalted is He, and some of you believe in Him, Mighty and Majestic is He. Alternatively, it means: some of you disbelieve in Him, glory be to Him, and some of you believe in Him, Exalted is He. This is a detailing (tafsil) of the generality (ijmal) in ﴿created you﴾, because the fact that some of them, or some among them, are disbelievers, and that some of them, or some among them, are believers, is intended by it. The fa' here is like its use in His words, ﴿And Allah created every creature from water; so of them is one that moves on its belly﴾ [al-Nur 24:45] and so on. Thus disbelief and belief are included within the act of creation. This is what the sound reports support, such as the report of al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud, from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) narrated to us, and he is the truthful one whose word is believed: "Indeed, the creation of each one of you is gathered in his mother's womb for forty days as a drop (nutfah), then it becomes a clinging clot (alaqah) for a similar period, then it becomes a lump of flesh (mudghah) for a similar period. Then Allah sends to it an angel with four words: his provision is written, his term, his deeds, and whether he is wretched or happy. Then the soul is breathed into him..." to the end of the hadith.

And Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the semen remains in the womb for forty nights, an angel of souls (malak al-nufus) comes to it and ascends with it to the Lord. He says: 'O Lord, is it male or female?' Allah decrees what He decrees. Then he says: 'Is it wretched or happy?' So he writes what he will meet."

Abu Dharr recited the first five verses of Surah al-Taghabun, up to the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿and He shaped you and made your shapes good, and to Him is the return﴾. The reconciling of the two reports is not hidden from anyone who has been given a share of knowledge. The mention of disbelief first is because it is the more prevalent.

Some scholars chose that the meaning is: He it is who created you in a wondrous creation, containing all the foundations of perfections, both intellectual and practical. Yet among you is one who chooses disbelief and acquires it, contrary to what his creation requires, and among you is one who chooses belief and acquires it, in accordance with what his creation requires. It was obligatory upon all of you to choose belief, thankful for the blessing of creation and bringing into existence and what branches from these two of the other blessings. But you did not do that, despite your full ability to do so; rather, you split into branches and separated into sects. This is the view taken by al-Zamakhshari. However, he explained "the disbeliever" as the one who comes with disbelief and performs it, and "the believer" as the one who comes with belief and performs it, because this is more suited to his school, which holds that the servant is the creator of his own acts. He also holds that the verse is to show their neglect of what the bestowal of the basic blessing, namely creation and bringing into existence, requires of them. The following verses are, in his view, a threat against disbelief and against denying that the Creator should be disobeyed and His blessing not be thanked. Then he said: How ignorant is the one who mixes disbelief with creation and makes it part of it, when creation is the greatest blessing from Allah the Exalted upon His servants, and disbelief is the greatest ingratitude from the servants toward their Lord, glory be to Him. Al-Tibi, on this reading, made the fa' indicate sequence and consequence, by way of metaphor (isti'arah), like the lam in His words, ﴿Then the people of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 28:8]. It is like the fa' in His words, ﴿And We placed in their offspring prophethood and the Book, and among them is one guided, but many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Hadid 57:26]. He did not take it as detailing, as has been said.

He chose, in the verse, the earlier meaning, supporting it with the sound hadiths and with the claim that the context supports it, asserting that all the verses are sent down to show the greatness of Allah the Exalted in His dominion and sovereignty, His sole authority over them, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, and His bringing into being the existents, both their essences and their accidents. His student, the meticulous author of al-Kashshaf, agreed with him in choosing this. He objected to al-Zamakhshari's words, "How ignorant is..." etc., by saying: "In it is what has passed many times," as if he meant the contradiction of the texts regarding disbelief not being created like other things. Moreover, the creation of disbelief is also among the great blessings, for were it not for its creation and the clarification of its harms, the measure of the blessing of belief and its benefits would not be manifest. Furthermore, its being disbelief is by reference to its subsistence in the servant, and from it comes ugliness, not by reference to its being created by Allah, as has been verified in its proper place. Then he said: From this it becomes clear that the strained interpretation of His words, ﴿so among you﴾ and so on, to take it out of being a detailing of the generality in ﴿created you﴾, is a distortion of the Book of Allah the Exalted. End of quote.

In my view, what favours the detailing in general is His words, "disbeliever and believer" (kafir wa mu'min), rather than "he who disbelieves and he who believes." Yet, the non-inclusion of disbelief and belief in creation is more consistent with His words, ﴿the nature of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum 30:30], and with the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every child is born upon the fitrah." The fair view is that the verse admits both meanings: the meaning mentioned first, and the meaning chosen by some. The context can be taken to fit each, and it is not explicit in either of the two matters you have heard, so that it is said that the verses come to explain what the promise and the threat depend upon afterward, of complete power and comprehensive knowledge over both worlds. His words, ﴿And Allah is seer of what you do﴾, meaning that He will recompense you accordingly, do not conflict with the creation of disbelief and belief, because both are acquired by the servant, and Allah's creating them does not conflict with their being acquired by the servant, as has been explained in the commentary on His words, ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾ [al-Saffat 37:96]. However, most of the hadiths support the first meaning. I think you would choose the second, because the setting being one of reproach for disbelief is more evident and better suited to it. It is reported from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: ﴿so among you is a disbeliever﴾, that is, a disbeliever in Allah who believes in the star, ﴿and among you is a believer﴾ in Allah who disbelieves in the star. It was also said: ﴿so among you is a disbeliever﴾ in the Creation, namely the Dahriyyah (materialists who deny a Creator and attribute events to time), ﴿and among you is a believer in it.⁠﴾ It is reported from al-Hasan that there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the intended sense is "and among you is a sinner (fasiq)." I do not think this is sound; it seems to be one of the lies of the Mu'tazilah against him. The sentence, according to what some learned scholars have inferred, is coordinated with the relative clause (silah). The absence of a returning pronoun (ha'id) does not harm it, because a fa'-coordinated clause is satisfied by the presence of the pronoun in one of the two clauses, as they have stated in examples such as "the one who flies so Zayd is angered, the fly." Or it may be said that there is a link by interpretation, meaning: among you is one whose disbelief has been decreed, and among you is one whose belief has been decreed. Or: ﴿so among you is a disbeliever﴾ in it, ﴿and among you is a believer﴾ in it, the ellipsis being understood gradually. It is also permitted that the coordination be with the clause ﴿He it is who created you﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 64, verse 3:

﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ — with the great wisdom, which includes the religious and worldly benefits. It is said: the original sense of ḥaqq (truth) is the opposite of bāṭil (falsehood), so by it is meant the sound purpose, realized in the most perfect manner, and that is the great wisdom.

﴿And He shaped you and perfected your shapes﴾ — for He created you in the best of forms, and deposited in you, of the outward and inward faculties and perceptions, that upon which all perfections, manifest and hidden, depend. He adorned you with the choicest of the attributes of His creatures, singled you out with the essence of the special qualities of His originated beings, and made you the model of all His creatures in this mode of existence. Some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) have mentioned that man combines the upper world (al-ʿalam al-ʿulwī) and the lower world (al-ʿalam al-suflī), because of his soul (rūḥ), which is of the world of immaterial things (al-mujarradāt), and his body (badan), which is of the world of material things (al-māddiyyāt). And they recited:

"You claim that you are a small body, yet in you the greatest world is folded up."

"By my life, man is the most wondrous copy in this world, comprising subtle secrets, some of which the signs (āthār) have borne witness to, and whatever of them the people of insight know."

Some scholars have restricted ṣūrah (form) to the shape perceived by the eye, as is well known. Every human form that is seen is beautiful, but beauty, like other meanings, has levels and ranks. Because some of them fall clearly below the ranks above them, and their being compared with what surpasses them is not considered pleasing, yet they are still included within the realm of beauty and not outside its limit. Do you not see that you may admire a form and find it pleasing, without it having captivated the world for you; then you see one more graceful and higher in the ranks of beauty, so your gaze turns away from the first, and you find looking at it burdensome after your infatuation with it and your ardent devotion to it. The wise have said: there are two things with no limit: beauty and eloquence.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Abū Razīn read ﹙ṣiwarakum﹚ with a kasra on the ṣād, whereas the analogical form is with a ḍammah, as in the reading of the majority.

﴿And to Him is the final return﴾ — in the other mode of existence, not to anything else, either independently or in partnership. So direct what has been created for you toward that for which He created you, lest what is seen of your beauty be disfigured by punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 64, verse 4:

﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾, of matters both universal and particular, and of states both manifest and hidden. ﴿And He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾, that is, what you keep secret among yourselves and what you make apparent of matters and openly declare, though this is included in what precedes it, for the sake of giving attention to its importance, because it is this on which recompense turns. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tirad tadhyili), confirming what precedes it regarding the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of their secret and their open affairs. That is, He, mighty and majestic, encompasses all the hidden things that dwell in the breasts of people, in such a way that they never depart from them at all; so how could what they keep secret and what they make known be hidden from Him, exalted is He? The mention of the Name Allah (al-Jalalah) serves to indicate the reason for the judgment and to emphasize the independence of the sentence. It has been said: the mention of confirming His power before His knowledge is because the indication of created things to His power, exalted is He, is in itself, and to His knowledge, glorified is He, is through what they contain of perfection and of specificity in certain respects.

And ʿUbayd, from Abu ʿAmr, and Aban, from ʿAsim, read ﴿mā yusirrūna wa-mā yuʿlinūna﴾ with the yā' of the third person (ghayba).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 64, verse 5:

﴿Has there not come to you﴾ — i.e., O disbelievers — the address being specified to them by what follows. The apparent meaning of the words of some of the eminent scholars (al-ajillah) is that what is meant by them are the people of Makkah, as if it were said: "Has there not come to you, O people of Makkah, ﴿the news of those who disbelieved before﴾ like the people of Nuh (Noah), Hud, Salih, and others of the nations that persisted in disbelief," ﴿so they tasted the evil consequence of their affair﴾ — i.e., the harm of their disbelief in this world, without delay. The root of wabal (evil consequence) is heaviness and severity that follows from a matter; from it comes al-wabil, for food that is heavy on the stomach, and al-wabil, for heavy rain with large drops. It is used for harm because it weighs upon a person with a non-physical heaviness. He expressed their disbelief as "affair" (amr) to signal that it is a monstrous matter and a great crime. ﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a painful punishment﴾ whose extent cannot be measured.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ That is, what was mentioned of the punishment they tasted in this world and what they will taste in the Hereafter. ﴿بِأنَّهُ﴾ That is, because of the fact that the matter [was such that].

﴿كانَتْ تَأْتِيهِمْ رُسُلُهم بِالبَيِّناتِ﴾ Their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, meaning the manifest miracles. ﴿فَقالُوا﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to ﴿كانَتْ﴾.

﴿أبَشَرٌ يَهْدُونَنا﴾ That is, each people of those peoples who disbelieved said, regarding their messenger who came to them with the miracles, denying that the messenger could be of the kind of humankind (bashar), or expressing amazement at that: "Is it a human who guides us?" As Thamud said: ﴿أبَشَرًا مِنّا واحِدًا نَتَّبِعُهُ﴾ (al-Qamar: 24). The narration has been summarized, so the speech is attributed to all the peoples, and "bashar" is intended as the category (jins), which is why it is described in the plural, just as the address has been summarized. The imperative in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿يا أيُّها الرُّسُلُ كُلُوا مِنَ الطَّيِّباتِ واعْمَلُوا صالِحًا﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 51) is similar. "Bashar" is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿يَهْدُونَنا﴾ is its predicate according to al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya. However, the better view is that it is in the nominative as the subject of a verb (fa'iliyya) with an elided verb that the mentioned verb explains, because the interrogative hamza is more inclined toward the verb, and the construction belongs to the category of ishtighal (the verb being "occupied" with a pronoun referring to the noun, so that the noun is governed by a verb that has been elided). ﴿فَكَفَرُوا﴾ They disbelieved in the messengers, peace be upon them. ﴿وتَوَلَّوْا﴾ They turned away from reflecting on what they were brought of clear proofs, and from believing in them. ﴿واسْتَغْنى اللَّهُ﴾ That is, Glorified is He, manifested His independence from their faith and their obedience, by destroying them and cutting off their line. Had He not been independent, Mighty and Majestic is He, of both, He would not have done that. The clause is conjoined to what precedes it. It has also been said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning ﴿فَكَفَرُوا وتَوَلَّوْا﴾ while God had been independent of all things, but the first is the preferred view. ﴿واللَّهُ غَنِيٌّ﴾ independent of the worlds, let alone of their faith and obedience. ﴿حَمِيدٌ﴾ praised by every creature through the tongue of state (lisan al-hal), which is more eloquent than the tongue of speech (lisan al-maqal). Or it means: He, Majestic is His standing, deserves praise in Himself, even if no one praises Him, Glorified is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 64, verse 7:

﴿Those who disbelieved claim that they will never be resurrected.﴾ Al-za'm (claim) is the assertion of knowledge, and it is most often used for a false assertion. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Shurayh that it is the kunya (figurative name) of falsehood, and it is well known that it is the mount (mattiyya) of falsehood. Because it carries the meaning of knowledge, it takes two objects, and here the two objects are filled by "an" (that) the lightened form (al-mukhaffafa) and what falls within its scope. The intended referent of the relative pronoun, according to al-Kashshaf, is the people of Makkah, so it is, as you have heard, the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun in the address. What apparently supports this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected.﴾ In al-Kashf he says: It is also possible that the reference is general, encompassing them and their likes, since the disbelievers of Makkah were mentioned first, and others who were made to take lesson from their condition. This is more eloquent. That is, they claimed that the matter is that they will never be resurrected after their death. ﴿Say⦆ in refutation of them and to make manifest the falsehood of their claim, by affirming what they denied: Yes, you will be resurrected. He emphasized this with the oath clause, so it falls within the scope of the command. Likewise the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then you will surely be informed of what you did﴾, that is, you will be called to account and recompensed for your deeds. This was added to explain the certainty of another matter that follows from the resurrection and depends on it, so it also contains emphasis for it. ﴿And that﴾, that is, what has been mentioned of the resurrection and recompense, ﴿is easy for Allah﴾, because of the certainty of complete power and the acceptance of the substance. The fa' in the saying of the Exalted:

﴿So believe﴾ is a *fa'* of explanation (*al-fa' al-mufassiḥah*, مُفَصَّحَةٌ), indicating a condition that has been omitted because its obviousness makes it clear, meaning: "if the matter is so," ﴿so believe in God﴾, who, as you have heard of His affairs, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿and His Messenger﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and the light which We have sent down﴾. This is the Qur'an, for by its inimitability it is manifest in itself and makes other things manifest, just as light does. The shift (*al-iltifāt*, الِالتِفاتُ, a change in grammatical person) to the first-person plural of majesty (*nūn al-ʿaẓamah*, نُونِ العَظَمَةِ, the "We" of majesty) serves to highlight the importance given to the matter of sending down, and in this is the exaltation of the status of the Qur'an to the extent that it contains. ﴿And God is aware of what you do﴾, of complying with the command and of abandoning it, ﴿All-Aware﴾, knowing its inner aspect.

The intended meaning is the perfection of His knowledge, exalted be He, of that. It is said: He is knowing of its news.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 64, verse 9:

﴿On the Day He gathers you﴾ is an adverbial of time (*zarf*) governed by ﴿you will surely be informed﴾. His statement, ﴿And that is easy for Allah﴾, and His statement, ﴿So believe﴾ up to ﴿well-Aware﴾, are parenthetical clauses (*i'tiraD*). The first affirms the power to resurrect, and the second emphasizes what the speech was directed toward: the exhortation to believe in Him, in what He revealed in the Book, and in the one who brought it. In reality, this is the conclusion of His statement, ﴿You will surely be resurrected, then you will surely be informed﴾. The adverbial was placed before its governed element (*ma'mul*) for emphasis, so it functions as a parenthetical clause. His statement, ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, is a parenthetical clause within a parenthetical clause, since it completes the exhortation to believe, just as one says: "Do what you will, for I will not forgive you."

Al-Hawfi said: The adverbial is governed by ﴿well-Aware﴾. According to more than one of the great scholars, it means "the One who will requite you," and so it includes both promise and threat.

Al-Zamakhshari took it to mean "the One who will punish you," then permitted this interpretation. It was objected that this does not merely signify threat but exhortation, since how could it be only a threat when the threat was already completed by His statement, ﴿You will surely be informed of what you did﴾? Therefore it is not fitting to render it as "the One who will punish you." Reflect on this.

It was also permitted that it be in the accusative by an implied verb, "remember" (*udhkur*). This was objected to as well: although it is fine, it is a deletion without any apparent indication.

It was further permitted that it be an adverbial of an implied element, indicated by the context, meaning: there will be among the states and terrors what no speech can encompass, on the Day He gathers you. This was objected to on the grounds that it involves an unnecessary deletion. Therefore the first interpretation is the more probable.

It is read as ﴿yajma'kum﴾ with the ayn sukun, and the present-tense verb with a plural object pronoun may be given a sukun. It is also reported with *ishmam* (partial rounding toward *damma*). Salam, Ya'qub, Zayd ibn Ali and al-Sha'bi read ﴿najma'kum﴾ with the letter nun.

﴿For the Day of Gathering﴾: for a Day on which the first and the last are gathered. It has been said that the angels and both groups (humans and jinn) are gathered. Other views have also been stated, but the first is the most apparent. The lam has been said to indicate reason (*lil-ta'lil*), and there is an implied elided noun (*mudaf muqaddar*), meaning: for the sake of the reckoning that takes place on the Day of Gathering. It has also been said that the lam means "in" (*bi-ma'na fi*), so no elision is needed.

﴿That is the Day of Mutual Loss-and-Gain﴾: 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada that they said: it is the day on which the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire were cheated (*ghubina*). The reciprocal form (*tafa'ul*) here is not on its literal sense, as in "tawaDu'" (mutual humility) and "tahamul" (mutual bearing of burden), since it occurs from one side only. It was chosen for emphasis (*mubalagha*). Al-Wahidi followed this view.

Others said: that is, the Day on which some people cheated others, by the descent of the blessed to the places of the wretched had they been blessed, and the reverse. In the Sahih it is related: "There is no servant who enters Paradise but is shown his seat in the Fire, had he done evil, so that he may increase in gratitude; and there is no servant who enters the Fire but is shown his seat in Paradise, had he done good, so that he may increase in regret."

This is a metaphor drawn from the mutual loss-and-gain of merchants in trade. There is in it a note of mockery toward the wretched, since they are not truly cheated in the case of the blessed, who descend to their places in Paradise while the wretched descend to theirs in the Fire. Alternatively, this was taken as mutual loss-and-gain by way of hyperbole, through the rhetorical device of *mushakala* (rhetorical correspondence). In this case the reciprocal form is on its literal sense, and this is good. However, the mutual loss-and-gain here is the mutual loss-and-gain of the blessed and the wretched in opposition. The better wording is the unrestricted one. The increase of the blessed in mutual loss-and-gain is established in the authentic collections. Muhyi al-Sunnah preferred this view, saying: "Tagabun (mutual loss-and-gain) is a reciprocal form from *ghabn*, which is the loss of a share. The one who is cheated (*maghbun*) is the one who is cheated regarding his family and his dwellings in Paradise. Thus every disbeliever will be seen to be cheated by abandoning faith, and every believer will be seen to be cheated by his shortcoming in good deeds."

Al-Tibi said: Al-Raghib also follows this view, saying: "*Ghabn* is that your companion is deprived in a transaction between you and him through some kind of concealment. If it concerns property, one says *ghubina fulan* (with the ghayn dammah and the ba' kasrah). If it concerns opinion, one says *ghabina* (with the ghayn fathah and the ba' kasrah). And 'the Day of Mutual Loss-and-Gain' is the Day of Resurrection, due to the manifestation of loss in the sale referred to in His statement: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207], and His statement: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], and His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77]. Thus it is known that they were cheated in what they abandoned of the transaction and in what they engaged in of it, all together." End of quotation.

The phrase is a nominal sentence (*mubtada' wa khabar*), with the definite article indicating the category (*lil-jins*). It indicates the magnitude of that day and that its mutual loss-and-gain is the true mutual loss-and-gain, not the mutual loss-and-gain of worldly affairs, however great and grand they may be.

﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness﴾: that is, a righteous deed. ﴿He will remove from him his misdeeds﴾: that is, Allah, Exalted is He, will remove from him his misdeeds on that Day. ﴿And admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾: that is, those who are determined to abide therein. The plural is according to the meaning of ﴿whoever﴾, just as the singular is according to its wording. Al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Ja'far, Talha, Nafi', Ibn Amir, al-Mufaddal from Asim, Zayd ibn Ali, and al-Hasan (with a variant from him) read ﴿nukaffir﴾ and ﴿nudkhil﴾ with the nun of majesty (*nun al-azamah*) in both.

﴿That﴾: that is, what has been mentioned of the expiation of misdeeds and the admission into gardens. ﴿Is the great success﴾, which has no success beyond it, for it encompasses salvation from the greatest destructions and the attainment of the most exalted desires.

[Page 124]

And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — they are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein forever. And wretched is the destination. (That is) the Fire.

And it seems that this verse and the one before it, because they contain the stations of the blessed and the wretched, are an explanation of "at-taghabun" (the mutual loss and gain of the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain), on the interpretation that it refers to the mutual loss of the two groups by way of contrast. And because it contains detail, it has taken the position of something different, so it is connected with the conjunction "wa" (and). Likewise, it is also (an explanation) in general terms, though upon this interpretation it is an explanation only in a general sense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 64, verse 11:

﴿No affliction befalls [anyone]﴾ i.e., no affliction befalls anyone. Here the object is elided, and "min" is extra (ziyadah), and "musibah" is the subject (fa'il). Omitting the ta' marbutah in such a construction is eloquent, but attaching it is more common, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"No community precedes its term"﴾ [al-Hijr: 5; al-Mu'minun: 43] and ﴿"No sign comes to them"﴾ [al-An'am: 4]. What is meant by "musibah" is calamity (raziyyah) and whatever distresses a servant, in self, property, child, speech, or action. I.e., no one is struck by any misfortune of this world, of whatever kind it may be, ﴿except by the permission of Allah﴾, i.e., by His will, glorified is He, and His enabling, mighty and majestic is He. It is as if the calamity itself is directed at the servant, yet contingent upon the will of Exalted Allah and His enabling, majestic and exalted is He.

It is also permissible that "musibah" be understood as any event, whether of evil or of good. They have explicitly stated that it is used for what befalls a servant of good and for what befalls him of evil. However, it was said: in the first sense it is from ṣawb, i.e., rain, and in the second from the striking of an arrow (isabat al-sahm). The first is the apparent meaning, although the ruling that it depends on permission is general.

﴿And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart﴾ at the time of its occurrence, to patience and "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" (istirja'), as it is said. According to 'Alqamah, [it is] for knowledge that it is from Allah, Exalted is He, so he submits to the command of Allah, Exalted is He, and is content with it. Something close to this is reported from Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿He guides his heart﴾ to certainty, so he knows that what befell him would not have missed him, and what missed him would not have befallen him. It was also said: ﴿He guides his heart﴾ i.e., He is gentle with him and expands his breast for increase in goodness and obedience.

Ibn Jubayr, Talhah, Ibn Hurmuz and al-Azraq from Hamzah read ﴿nahdi﴾ with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah).

al-Sulami, al-Dahhak and Abu Ja'far read ﴿yuhda﴾ with the ya', in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ul), with ﴿qalbuhu﴾ in the nominative as a substitute for the subject (naybah 'an al-fa'il). It was also read likewise but with ﴿qalbihi﴾ in the accusative. This was explained as meaning that the subject's substitute is the pronoun of "man," and "qalbahu" is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), i.e., "yuhda fi qalbihi" or "yuhda ila qalbihi," in the sense that the disbeliever is astray from his heart and far from it, while the believer finds it and is guided to it, like His saying: ﴿for whoever has a heart﴾ [Qaf: 37]. Thus the statement involves elision and transitivity (hadhf wa-l-iysal), like ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6]. In it, the heart is placed in the position of the destination: whoever goes astray has been prevented from it, and whoever arrives has been guided to it. It is also permissible that its accusative be a specification (tamyiz), on the basis that it may be definite.

'Ikrimah, 'Amr ibn Dinar and Malik ibn Dinar read ﴿yahda'﴾ with a silent hamzah, ﴿qalbuhu﴾ in the nominative, meaning his heart becomes tranquil and settled through faith, with no unease or agitation in it. 'Amr ibn Fa'id read ﴿yahda﴾ with an alif replacing the silent hamzah; and 'Ikrimah and Malik ibn Dinar also read ﴿yahda﴾ by deleting the alif after its substitution for the hamzah. The substitution of hamzah in such cases is not analogical, according to Abu Hayyan, though some permitted it as analogical, and on this is built the permissibility of deleting that alif for the jussive (al-jazim). On this is based the verse of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma:

"Bold: whenever he wrongs, he is punished for his wrong swiftly; and if he does not begin with wrong, he is not wronged."

Its original form is yabda', the hamzah was replaced by an alif, then it was deleted for the jussive, by analogy with the alif of yakhsha when the jussive enters upon it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is, of everything﴾ among the things of which hearts and their states are a part, ﴿Knowing﴾. So He knows the faith of the believer and guides his heart at the time of affliction. Thus the sentence is connected to His saying: ﴿And whoever believes﴾, etc. It is also permissible that it be connected to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿No affliction befalls﴾, etc., as a concluding statement (tadhyil) to it, for confirmation and emphasis. al-Tibi mentioned that in the words of al-Kashshaf there is an allusion that the verse contains an elision: i.e., whoever does not believe, He does not show gentleness to him, or does not guide his heart; and whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart. On this it is built that the affliction includes disbelief and sins as well, since they occur after the recompense of the believer and the disbeliever, and are followed by the matter that comes next; and what affliction is greater than these? And this, as he indicated, repels the Mu'tazilah in their throats.

﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾. He repeated the command for emphasis and to indicate the difference between the two obediences in their manner (al-ta'kid, emphasis). It also clarifies the object of turning away in His saying, ﴿But if you turn away﴾, i.e., from obedience to the Messenger. His saying, ﴿Then the duty of Our Messenger is only clear notification﴾, is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of the omitted response (al-jawab al-mahdhuf, the implied apodosis of the conditional), which it has taken the place of. That is: there is no blame upon him, since his only duty is clear notification, and he has fulfilled it in a manner beyond which nothing more can be asked. The mention of "the Messenger" as an explicit noun, attributed to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah, the royal "We"), in a place where a pronoun would be expected, is to honour him, peace and blessings be upon him, and to indicate the basis of the ruling, which is that his function, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is purely clear notification. It also serves to intensify the reprehensibility of turning away from him. The restriction (al-hasr) in the statement is relative (idafi).

Allah — there is no god but Him. The discussion of this phrase is like the discussion of the statement of tawhid (kalimat al-tawhid), and it has passed and is sweet. ﴿And upon Allah﴾, that is, upon Him, may He be exalted, specifically and to the exclusion of other than Him, neither independently nor in partnership. ﴿So let the believers put their trust﴾. The display of the Divine Name (al-Jalalah) in the place where a pronoun would be expected is to indicate the reason for trust (tawakkul). Or [it is] the command to it: for divinity (al-uluhiyyah) necessitates devoting oneself wholly to Him, may He be exalted, and cutting off attachment entirely to all else among creatures. Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that the restriction of the command to trust to the believer is because faith that everything is from Him, may He be exalted, necessitates trust. From here it was said: "Among the verses, there is none greater than this verse for one who reflects on the exhortation to trust, because it alludes to the fact that whoever does not trust in Allah, may He be exalted, is not a believer." And it is, as al-Tibi said, like the conclusion and summary of what preceded it, and like a bridge leading to another point of discourse.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 64, verse 14:**

﴿O you who believe, indeed among your spouses and your children are enemies to you﴾. That is, some of them are so. Among the spouses are wives who oppose their husbands, quarrel with them and stir up trouble against them. Among the children are some who oppose their fathers, disobey them and make them swallow grief and harm. We have witnessed wives who killed their husbands, others who ruined their husbands' minds by feeding them some substances that corrupt the mind, others who broke the vessel of their honour, and others who tore the bag of their wealth, and so on. Likewise, among the children there are those who have done the same. ﴿So beware of them﴾, that is, be on your guard against them and do not feel safe from their harms and their evil. The pronoun refers to "enemy", since the word is applied to the plural, as in the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 77]. So the command to beware applies to all of them. Or the pronoun refers to spouses and children together, so the command to beware is either to beware of some of them, because some of them are not enemies, or to beware of the whole of both groups, because both include enemies.

﴿And if you pardon﴾ their sins that are amenable to pardon, in that they relate to worldly matters, or to religious matters that are accompanied by repentance, in that you do not punish them for them. ﴿And overlook﴾, that is, turn away by abandoning reproach and rebuke. ﴿And forgive﴾, that is, conceal them by hiding them and smoothing the way for their excuse regarding them. ﴿Then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. This serves in place of the response to the condition. The meaning is that He will deal with you in the same manner as you have acted, and will show favour to you, for He, mighty and majestic is He, is ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾. Since the religious obligation (taklif) here is difficult, because the harm that comes from one to whom you have shown kindness is more painful in its sting and more likely to provoke retaliation, the emphasis in His words, glorified is He, ﴿And if you pardon﴾ and so on, is appropriate.

Some scholars have said: their enmity lies in the fact that they stand between their family and acts of obedience and things beneficial to them in the Hereafter. They may also drive them to strive for the acquisition of what is unlawful and the commission of sins for the sake of their own benefit, as has been reported from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "A time will come upon my nation when a man's ruin will be at the hand of his wife and his child, who reproach him for poverty, so he will mount the mounts of evil and be destroyed."

Some people are carried by their love for them and their compassion towards them to want them to live in comfort during his life and after his death, so he commits prohibited acts to obtain what will be a cause of that, even if they have not asked it of him, and so he is destroyed. The occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) is more in accord with this view.

Al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Jarir and others related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: This verse, ﴿O you who believe, indeed among your spouses﴾ and so on, was revealed concerning a people from Makkah who had embraced Islam and wished to come to the Prophet (ﷺ), but their wives and children refused to let them go. When they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and saw that the people had gained understanding in the religion, they wanted to punish their families. So Allah revealed the verse. In another report from him, he said: A man would want to emigrate, but his wife and child would hold him back. He would say: "By Allah, if Allah gathers me and you in the abode of emigration, I will certainly do such and such." Then Allah, mighty and majestic is He, gathered them together in the abode of emigration, and Allah revealed ﴿O you who believe, indeed among your spouses﴾ the verse.

It was also said: They said to them, "If Allah gathers us in the abode of emigration, we will not give you any good." When they emigrated, they withheld good from them, so the verse was revealed. It is related from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah that 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i wished to join the raid with the Prophet (ﷺ), but his family and children gathered and discouraged him and complained to him about being parted from him. He was softened and did not go on the raid. Then he regretted it and resolved to punish them, so the verse was revealed. It has been cited as evidence that a man should not harbour resentment against his wife and child when they commit a wrong together with him, nor should he invoke curses upon them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 64, verse 15:

﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ i.e., a test,

and an affliction, because they lead to falling into sin, worldly hardships, and other things. In a hadith: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'His dependents have consumed his good deeds.'" And it is related from some of the salaf (the early righteous generations): "Dependents are the worms that eat away at acts of obedience."

Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim related, and he authenticated it, from Buraydah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon when al-Hasan and al-Husayn came toward him, wearing two red shirts, walking and stumbling. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came down from the pulpit, picked them up, one on each side, and then climbed the pulpit again and said: 'Allah has spoken the truth: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾. When I looked at these two boys walking and stumbling, I could not be patient, so I cut off my speech and came down to them.'"

In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Abdullah ibn Umar: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon to the people from the pulpit, al-Husayn ibn Ali came out toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he stepped on a garment he was wearing and fell, and he wept. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came down from the pulpit, and when the people saw him, they hurried toward al-Husayn, passing him from one to another until he fell into the hands of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'May Allah fight Satan! Indeed, the child is a trial. By Him in whose hand my soul is, I did not realize that I had come down from my pulpit.'"

It has also been said: if jihad and emigration are possible for you, then let your inclination toward wealth and children not tempt you away from them. Al-Kashf said: "The trial in this interpretation is the inclination toward wealth and children, without punishment or sin." Wealth is mentioned first, and it was said: "Because it is the greater trial." ﴿Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6–7]. Ahmad, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Tirmidhi related, and he authenticated it, from Ka'b ibn Iyad, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Every nation has a trial, and the trial of my nation is wealth.'"

Ibn Mardawayh related something similar from Abdullah ibn Awfa, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). It seems that, because the trial in wealth and children is predominant, the partitive "min" was not mentioned here as it was in what preceded. ﴿And Allah has with Him a great reward﴾ for the one who prefers the love of Allah and His obedience over the love of wealth and children and the pursuit of their welfare in a manner that undermines that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 64, verse 16:

﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾: that is, exert your utmost effort and capacity in being mindful of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, as transmitted by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, and it is related from Abu al-ʿAliyah.

Ibn Abi Ḥatim transmitted from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: When ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ [Al ʿImran: 102] was revealed, the act of worship became burdensome for the people, so they stood (in prayer) until their ankles swelled and their foreheads were chafed. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed, as a relief for the Muslims, ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾, and so the earlier verse was abrogated (naskh). Something similar is reported from Qatadah. From Mujahid, the meaning is that He should be obeyed and not disobeyed. Most (scholars) hold that this is the intended meaning in the verse we have cited.

﴿And listen﴾ to His admonitions, the Exalted, ﴿and obey﴾ His commands, the Mighty and Majestic, and His prohibitions, the Glorified, ﴿and spend﴾ from what He has provided you, in the ways He has commanded you to spend, sincerely for His Face, Exalted is His glory, as indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿better for yourselves﴾. The mention of this is a specification after a generalization. The word ﴿khayran﴾ (better) is in the accusative according to Sibawayh, as the direct object of a deleted verb: "And bring about good for your souls," meaning, do what is better and more beneficial for them. This is an emphasis on urging the carrying out of these commands, and a clarification that these matters are better for their souls than wealth and children. There is in this a trace of tajrid (a stylistic device of abstraction). According to Abu ʿUbayd, it is the predicate of a deleted "yakun" (let it be), as an answer to the imperative, meaning: "let it be good." According to al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i, it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: "a good spending." It has also been said that it is accusative by "anfiqu" (spend), and that "al-khayr" means wealth, though this is remote in meaning. Some Kufan grammarians said it is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥal), but this is remote both in meaning and in grammatical analysis (iʿrab).

﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul﴾, which is miserliness together with greed.

﴿Those are the successful﴾, the ones who attain every desired goal.

Page 128

If you lend to Allah a goodly loan (﴿إنْ تُقْرِضُوا اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا﴾), i.e., you spend wealth on the channels (al-masarif) that He, Mighty and Majestic, has designated. In the speech there is a metaphorical analogy (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), [the loan being a figure for spending in the way of Allah]. "A goodly loan" is one accompanied by sincerity and a contented soul. ﴿He will multiply it for you﴾, i.e., He, exalted is His majesty, will make for you, for every one, ten up to seven hundred and more. It is also read as "yudh'ifhu" (yud'ifhu). ﴿And will forgive you﴾ by the blessing of spending what has passed from you of some sins. ﴿And Allah is Appreciative﴾, giving abundantly in return for a small and meagre amount. ﴿Forbearing﴾, not hastening to punish despite the abundance of sins.

(Verse 18 of Surah 64, continued from the commentary of al-Alusi in Ruh al-Ma'ani:)

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: nothing is hidden from Him, glory be to Him. ﴿The Almighty, the Wise﴾: the One who is perfect in power and wisdom. In the verse there is encouragement to spend (infaq) of what it contains; however, scholars differed regarding what is meant by it. It was said: it refers to obligatory spending, namely the obligatory zakat, and this has been explicitly stated. It was said: it refers to recommended spending. It was said: it includes all of these. And God knows best.
